newsitem.title: UK: Chancellor gives clues to first budget.
newsitem.headline: Chancellor gives clues to first budget.

text.p: Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown has given some public clues as to his thinking about his first budget.

He said it would be a "welfare-to-work" budget, with a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities as its centrepiece. The proceeds will fund a programme to create 250,000 jobs for the young and long-term unemployed.
Brown has also promised to reduce value-added tax on domestic fuel bills to five percent from eight.
He pledged to stick to existing spending limits set by the previous government for the next two years and not to increase income tax rates for five years.
Labour's campaign manifesto listed a long-term objective of a 10 pence starting rate of income tax but Brown has given no indication when this might be introduced.
Following is a selection of Gordon Brown's public comments on economic and fiscal policy this year

January 20, 1997 -- "I want to make it clear we will not increase the basic rate of tax. It is because we understand the importance of work that there will be no return to penal marginal tax rates at the top."
"Our commitment to fairness means we will cut VAT on fuel to five percent -- the lowest level allowed."
"In 1994, I reaffirmed that we would not extend VAT to food, children's clothes and shoes, books and newspapers and public transport fares. That remains the position."
"As a signal of our intentions, I want to make clear that we will not introduce a new top rate of (income) tax."

"My tax-cutting ambition is to introduce a new lower starting rate of tax of 10p to encourage people to go back to work and help all hard-working families. This will be matched by a cut in the benefit tapers to ensure that those receiving benefits are also rewarded by the new lower rate"
"Our first budget will not reopen overall spending allocations (for government departments) for the 1997-98 financial year."

"While government still has and must have a clear responsibility to advance the public interest, we do not make the mistake of equating this with a commitment to inexorable increases in public spending."

January 31, 1997 -- "I am determined to create a platform for stability by implementing credible anti-inflationary policies which convince people that they can expect stable, non-inflationary growth."
February 13, 1997 -- "We want to move quickly on this (the Windfall Tax). It will be in a first budget, the budget will come within a few weeks of the general election."
March 26, 1997 -- "Labour's minimum wage is a vital component of a strategy that will create jobs."
April 17, 1997 -- "There should be no power to raise taxes removed from Britain to Europe, no power to decide on spending issues to be removed. We've made that absolutely clear over a long period."
April 22, 1997 -- "People know that the privatised utilities who will be affected are those ... regulated by statute. Only those companies who have made excess profits will pay the tax."

May 1, 1997 -- "I have said the budget will be within two months. It is a budget to equip this country for the future. I made...commitments - one on the basic and top rate of tax, one on cutting VAT on fuel, which we will do in the first budget, so it will be in by the winter fuel bills for pensioners."

May 2, 1997 (the day after Labour's landslide election win) -- "People are right to say we must avoid the inflationary pressures that could exist at this time of the economic cycle. We must also tackle the problem of social security bills which have put an additional pressure on both borrowing and taxation."

May 6, 1997 (the day Brown raised interest rates and announced the Bank of England would be free to set rates from then on) -- "We must break from the short-termism of the past and the economic instability that has characterised the British economy, not just in recent years but for most of the century."
"My judgment is that we have inherited a situation in which, in the absence of corrective action, inflation will overshoot the government's inflation target next year."

On cutting VAT on heating fuel: "It is the law. We will be able to do it. I am absolutely certain it is possible and we will do it and I have already said we are going to legislate in the first Budget."

May 11, 1997 -- "I am not interested in measures that just alleviate the problem of youth and long-term unemployment for a few months. I am interested in developing a welfare state built around the work ethic."
May 12, 1997 -- "There has been no change in our position. We have no plans to re-join the ERM."
May 20, 1997 -- "I said right at the beginning of my term as Chancellor that I wanted to plan for monetary stability for the long term, hence my reforms of the Bank of England."

"There must be honest finances as well as sound finances. I think people right across the country will welcome the fact that the books are being opened to an independent body (the National Audit Office) which will look at these matters and report on them."
"There will be openness as well as soundness in the public finances. We have only made promises that we can keep and the promises we have made we will keep and I am determined on that."

"We will identify the barriers to growth and productivity and then we will relentlessly work to remove them. Stability is necessary for our future economic success. But stability for the long-term needs to be matched, in my view, by a new drive for dynamism and adaptability in industry, and by a new approach from government to wealth creation, employment and welfare."
